subtitle: Classifying postulates and theorems, applying a postulate, testing the truth of a converse, and deciding when a biconditional is valid

problems.note: Segment Addition Postulate: AB + BC = AC with AB = 2x+3, BC = 3x-1, AC = 27.

problems.desc: Classify five statements as definition, postulate or theorem and give the deciding reason for each - reasoning answer, read the student's classification and justification

problems.note: Angle Addition Postulate: m(ABD) + m(DBC) = m(ABC) with 4x, 3x+5 and 96.
Converse of 'if x = 6 then x^2 = 36' is false: the full solution set is -6 and 6.
The solution set of 2x - 7 = 9 is exactly {8}, so the biconditional holds both ways.
Two congruent but adjacent angles, (5x-8) and (3x+22), disprove the converse of the Vertical Angles Theorem.

problems.desc: Explain why 'through any two points there is exactly one line' is taken as a postulate while 'two intersecting lines meet in exactly one point' is a theorem, and describe what a proof of the second one would rest on - reasoning answer, read the student's explanation

problems.note: Perpendicular-bisector biconditional: P is on the perpendicular bisector of AB iff PA = PB, with PA = 4x-5 and PB = 2x+7.

problems.desc: Write the converse of 'if a quadrilateral is a square then it has four right angles', decide whether the converse is true, and support the decision with a labelled counterexample - reasoning answer, read the student's converse and counterexample

Rewrite the definition of an angle bisector as a biconditional, then decide whether 'if two angles are complementary then they are adjacent' can be written as a valid biconditional and justify the decision - reasoning answer, read the student's biconditional and justification
